summary:

- Company and listing details: Delaware corporation (EIN 80-0429876) headquartered at 1455 Market Street, Suite 600, San Francisco, CA 94103; phone (415) 375-3176. Class A Common Stock (par value $0.0000001) listed on the New York Stock Exchange; no securities registered under Section 12(g).
- Filer and compliance status: well-known seasoned issuer; large accelerated filer; not a smaller reporting company; not a shell company. Confirmed timely filing of required reports and submission of Interactive Data Files (XBRL). Disclosure of delinquent filers not included.
- Equity and ownership data: aggregate market value of non-affiliate common equity approximately $1.4 billion as of June 30, 2016. Shares outstanding as of February 17, 2017: 208,288,497 Class A and 158,902,579 Class B. Portions of the Definitive Proxy Statement for the Annual Meeting are incorporated by reference into Part III (to be filed within 120 days of fiscal year end).

- Special Note Regarding Forward-Looking Statements: cautions about statements concerning future financial performance, growth strategies (including GPV and revenue), technology and product development, international expansion, intellectual property, litigation expectations, and liquidity/capital resources. Emphasizes associated risks and uncertainties (see Risk Factors) and disclaims any obligation to update such statements except as required by law.

heading: PART I
start_phrase:
We
 started Square in February 2009 to enable businesses (sellers) to accept card payments, an important capability that was previously inaccessible to many
 businesses.
summary:
- Overview and mission: Square, founded in February 2009, aims to economically empower businesses by giving them accessible, affordable tools to accept payments and run their operations within a cohesive commerce ecosystem.
- Differentiation and design: Combines sophisticated software with affordable hardware to turn mobile/computing devices into POS systems; emphasizes fast, self-serve, dependable products and robust risk management using data science and machine learning, achieving high seller acceptance with low fraud losses.
- Core payments platform: Full-service managed payments with rapid onboarding; accepts in-person magstripe (swipe), EMV (dip), NFC (tap), and online via Square Invoices, Virtual Terminal, and merchant websites; provides reporting/analytics, next-day settlements, digital receipts, dispute management/chargeback protection, and PCI compliance.
- Consumer side: Square Cash enables individuals to send and receive money with people and businesses.
- Point-of-sale software and services: Tools for analytics and reporting; order, inventory, location, employee, and payroll management; customer engagement features; monetized via per-transaction, subscription, or service fees.
- Financial services: Square Capital facilitates business loans based on sellers’ processing histories.
- Platform and vertical solutions: Build with Square APIs for customized solutions and third-party integrations; vertical-specific tools such as Invoices, Appointments, and Inventory; Caviar food ordering service helps restaurants reach new customers.
- Scale and markets: Serves millions of sellers across retail, services, and food sectors, from sole proprietors to multi-location businesses in the U.S., Canada, Japan, and Australia.
- Volume and growth metrics: Processed $49.7B GPV in 2016 (1B card payments from ~245M cards), up from $35.6B in 2015 and $23.8B in 2014.
- Growth strategy: Efficient seller acquisition with strong cross-sell/up-sell opportunities; growing presence among larger sellers (annualized GPV > $125,000), which accounted for 42% of GPV in Q4 2016, up from 39% in Q4 2015.

title: Business
heading: Item 1. Business
start_phrase: We started Square in February 2009 to enable businesses (sellers) to accept card payments, an important capability that was previously inaccessible tomany businesses.
summary:
- Company overview and mission: Square (founded 2009) aims to economically empower sellers with an integrated, accessible commerce ecosystem to start, run, and grow their businesses.
- Cohesive ecosystem: Full-service managed payments as the foundation; fast onboarding; in-person (swipe, dip, tap) and online (Invoices, Virtual Terminal, e-commerce) acceptance; buyer-facing Square Cash for P2P and business payments.
- Hardware: Free magstripe reader; contactless and chip reader; chip card reader; Square Stand with peripheral support.
- Point-of-sale software and services: Square Point of Sale with Dashboard analytics; employee/location management, timecards, Payroll; customer engagement (feedback, marketing, loyalty); vertical solutions (Appointments, Invoices, Inventory); new Square for Retail with advanced inventory, PO, COGS, barcode scanning, clienteling.
- Developer platform: “Build with Square” APIs (POS, e-commerce, items/inventory, reporting/analytics, employee management) and App Marketplace integrations (e.g., QuickBooks, BigCommerce).
- Square Capital: Loan facilitation via partner bank using real-time payment/POS data; automated repayments as a % of card sales; majority funding via forward-flow sales to institutional investors; since May 2014, 200,000+ loans/MCAs totaling $1.3B.
- Caviar: Restaurant delivery marketplace expanding seller reach; fees to consumers (delivery/service) and restaurants (seller fee); active in multiple U.S. markets.
- Monetization: Transaction fees (transparent, covering reporting, next-day or instant settlement, receipts, dispute management, PCI); plus subscriptions and service fees for advanced features; transaction-based revenue as % of GPV was 2.93% (2016), 2.95% (2015), 2.98% (2014); instant deposit available for an extra fee.
- Scale and financials: 2016 GPV $49.7B (vs. $35.6B in 2015, $23.8B in 2014); about 1B card payments from ~245M cards in 2016; 2016 total net revenue $1.709B (up 35% YoY), adjusted revenue $686.6M (up 52% YoY); 2016 net loss $(171.6)M; adjusted EBITDA $44.9M; larger sellers (> $125k annualized GPV) were 42% of Q4’16 GPV; diversified seller base across industries and geographies (U.S., Canada, Japan, Australia); no customer >10% of GPV or net revenue in 2016.
- Seller base and growth: Efficient seller acquisition, cross-sell/upsell opportunities, growing penetration of larger sellers.
- Sales and marketing: Strong brand with NPS ~70; multi-channel direct marketing; retail distribution in 36,000+ stores (e.g., Apple, Amazon, Best Buy, Staples, Target, Walgreens); direct sales for larger sellers; partnerships and developer ecosystem; ongoing in-product communications and communities.
- Technology and product development: Mobile-first, platform-agnostic; tightly integrated hardware/software/payments; biweekly software releases; scalable platform with heavy use of data science and machine learning (automated risk assessment for >99.95% of transactions); in-house hardware design, third-party manufacturing; 2016 product development expense $268.5M.
- Transaction processing model: Roles and flow across PSP (Square), acquiring processors/banks, card networks, and issuing banks; fee components include processor fees, network assessments (<0.15% typically), and interchange (averaging 1.5%–2.0% plus fixed per transaction, varying by card/transaction); settlement timelines (next-day ACH or same-day instant deposit), ACH fees minimal; Square is merchant of record.
- Competition: Traditional acquirers/payment processors (often costly, long-term contracts); point solutions in POS/analytics/inventory/marketing; alternative lenders; delivery services; P2P providers. Square differentiates on an integrated, cohesive, self-serve, dependable ecosystem.
- Intellectual property: Mixed protections (patents, trademarks, copyrights, trade secrets, contracts); as of Dec 31, 2016, 229 issued patents and 588 applications globally (expiring 2022–2035); active trademark/domain strategy; uses some third-party and open-source technology.
- Regulation and compliance: U.S. money transmission licensing and FinCEN MSB registration; localized international services (Canada, Japan, Australia) with local oversight (e.g., AUSTRAC); consumer financial protection (CFPB and others); AML program and sanctions compliance; privacy/data protection; communications regulations for emails/SMS; other evolving areas (product liability, import/export, accessibility, insurance, marketing, labor/tax for Payroll expansion).
- Employees and corporate info: 1,853 full-time employees as of Dec 31, 2016; non-unionized; HQ in San Francisco; incorporated in Delaware (2009); investor relations and SEC filing access info; use of website/Twitter for disclosures.
- Early risk factors: Dependence on a strong, trusted brand; potential slowdown in growth tied to seller retention/acquisition and product adoption; ongoing net losses with continued investment may delay or prevent profitability.

summary:
- Context: Excerpt from Item 1A. Risk Factors of an Annual Report on Form 10-K (Risks Related to Our Business and Our Industry), warning that investing involves significant risk and that adverse events could materially affect the business and stock price.
- Brand and trust risk: The company’s success relies on maintaining a strong, trusted brand. Negative publicity; product/service quality or reliability issues; risk management shortcomings; complaint resolution failures; privacy/security incidents; litigation or regulatory actions; and misconduct by employees or partners could damage reputation, reduce confidence, and hurt usage.
- Growth sustainability risk: Future growth may slow or decline. Retention and expansion of existing sellers, acquisition of new sellers (including larger ones), and increased seller engagement are uncertain. Sellers lack long-term contracts and can switch easily; their processing volume may drop due to satisfaction, support, pricing, competition, macroeconomic conditions, or lower end-customer spending. New products and services (e.g., Square Cash, Caviar, Instant Deposit, Invoices) may not succeed.
- Financial performance and profitability risk: Despite revenue growth ($850.2M in 2014; $1,267.1M in 2015; $1,708.7M in 2016), the company has incurred net losses ($154.1M in 2014; $212.0M in 2015; $171.6M in 2016) and had an accumulated deficit of $779.2M as of December 31, 2016. Ongoing substantial investments (hiring, sales and marketing including direct marketing, referral programs, free hardware and subsidies, product development, office/infrastructure expansion, and international growth) may prevent achieving or maintaining profitability.

heading: Our business has generated net losses, and we intend to continue to invest substantially in our business. Thus, we may not be able to achieve or maintain profitability.
start_phrase: We generated net losses of $171.6 million, $212.0 million, and $154.1 million for the years ended December 31, 2016, 2015 and 2014, respectively.
summary:
- Excerpt is from Item 1A. Risk Factors of a Form 10-K, warning that investing involves significant risk that could materially harm the business and stock price.
- Brand and reputation risk: The company’s success depends on maintaining a strong, trusted brand; negative publicity, product/service quality issues, data protection or compliance failures, litigation, and misconduct by employees or partners could erode trust and usage.
- Growth sustainability risk: Although revenue grew from 2014–2016, the growth rate is expected to decline. Retention of existing sellers, acquisition of new and larger sellers, and increased usage are not assured due to no long-term contracts, low switching costs, competitive pricing/quality, support effectiveness, macro conditions, and variable customer spend. Dependence on the success of new products (e.g., Square Cash, Caviar, Instant Deposit, Invoices).
- Profitability risk and investment needs: History of net losses and a substantial accumulated deficit; plans to continue heavy investment in headcount, sales and marketing (including free/subsidized hardware/services), product development, infrastructure/office space, international expansion, and public company compliance. Upfront seller acquisition costs vs. later revenue recognition may increase losses; marketing and partner fees may rise. Management may prioritize long-term benefits over short-term results, which may not meet investor expectations.
- Data privacy and security risk: The company, sellers, partners, and service providers process large volumes of sensitive personal, payment, banking, business performance, and (in certain products) protected health information (HIPAA). Despite security measures and contractual safeguards, breaches or improper access/disclosure via third-party action, employee error, malware/phishing/hacking, or system issues could damage reputation, trigger significant liability, regulatory scrutiny and penalties, remediation costs, and card network liabilities (e.g., card reissuance). Breaches at vendors can have similar impacts.
- Platform reliability/security risk: As a core aspect of the business, any perceived or actual security breach could drive seller churn, hinder acquisition, require significant remediation spend, and expose the company to investigations, class actions, and fraud monitoring costs.
- Risk management and fraud/AML exposure: Offering managed payments to many customers requires effective vetting and monitoring; processing illegitimate transactions can cause losses, liabilities, regulatory sanctions, and partner contractual breaches. The automated, liquid nature of payments attracts misuse (fraud, money laundering, terrorist financing), including identity theft and use of stolen or fabricated payment credentials.

heading: Our risk management efforts may not be effective, which could expose us to losses and liability and otherwise harm our business.
start_phrase: We offer managed payments and other products and services to a large number of customers, and we are responsible for vetting and monitoring these customers and determining whether the transactions we process for them are legitimate.
summary:
- Rising operating costs: increasing expenses for acquiring and supporting new/larger sellers, public-company compliance, and advertising; upfront seller onboarding costs versus later revenue recognition may prolong losses if revenue growth and expense control lag.
- Long-term trade-offs: strategic choices made to improve seller and user experience may depress short-term results, conflict with investor expectations, and may not deliver anticipated long-term benefits.
- Data security and privacy risks: extensive collection and processing of sensitive data (PII, PCI data, bank details, seller performance data, PHI) across the company, sellers, partners, and third-party data centers; HIPAA obligations; potential breaches via malware, phishing, hacking, or errors could damage reputation, trigger regulatory scrutiny, penalties, remediation costs, and liability (including card reissuance costs); exposure also if company confidential information is disclosed.
- Platform security dependence: the reliability and security of the payments platform are critical; real or perceived breaches could cause seller loss, hinder new seller acquisition, drive significant remediation spend, and lead to legal and regulatory actions; third-party provider breaches pose similar risks.
- Risk management limitations: responsibility to vet and monitor customers and transactions; exposure to fraud, money laundering, and terrorist financing; inherent security–convenience trade-offs; growing exposure with larger sellers and new markets/products; potential inaccuracies in forecasting losses; ineffective policies or errors could result in major financial losses and civil/criminal liability.
- Chargebacks and refunds exposure: liability when disputes resolve against sellers or when sellers cannot reimburse (e.g., insolvency); EMV liability shift increases seller responsibility and reimbursement needs; not all readers are EMV-compliant; absence of seller reserves and occasional waivers increase risk; excessive chargebacks could lead to network fines, higher fees, or loss of card acceptance.
- Revenue concentration and diversification risk: heavy reliance on managed payments transaction fees; efforts to expand products/services and markets may fail, slow growth, introduce operational/technical challenges, service disruptions, and may not recoup investments, harming reputation and business.
- Need for continuous innovation: success depends on delivering enhancements and new features amid rapid changes in payments/POS, financial and marketing services; evolving technologies include e-commerce, mobile commerce, contactless/NFC, cryptocurrencies, and tokenization; failure to keep pace could materially and adversely affect the business.

title: We are currently, and will continue to be, exposed to risks associated with chargebacks and refunds in connection with payment card fraud or relating to the goods or services provided by our sellers.
heading: We are currently, and will continue to be, exposed to risks associated with chargebacks and refunds in connection with payment card fraud or relating to the goods or services provided by our sellers.
start_phrase: In the event that a billing dispute between a cardholder and a seller is not resolved in favor of the seller, including in situations where the seller engaged in fraud, the transaction is typically “charged back” to the seller and the purchase price is credited or otherwise refunded to the cardholder.
summary:
- Balancing security and customer convenience in payments creates inherent trade-offs; current risk management policies, procedures, and processes may not capture all existing or emerging risks.
- Concentration risk increases as larger sellers use the platform; domestic and international growth places ongoing demands on risk infrastructure and capabilities.
- Entering new services or markets with limited fraud history impairs loss forecasting and reserving; ineffective risk controls could lead to large financial losses, civil/criminal liability, and material business harm.
- Significant exposure to chargebacks and refunds from payment card fraud and seller-related issues; if sellers cannot or will not reimburse (e.g., bankruptcy or closure), the company may absorb losses.
- Post-October 2015 EMV liability shift increases seller responsibility for certain fraudulent chip-card transactions; not all offered readers are EMV-compliant, raising reimbursement needs and potential losses.
- The company does not maintain seller reserves for chargebacks and sometimes waives reimbursement for customer relations; sellers promising future delivery pose heightened chargeback risk.
- Excessive chargebacks could trigger payment network fines, higher transaction fees, or termination of card processing capabilities, materially harming the business.
- Revenue is highly concentrated in transaction-based fees from managed payments; diversification efforts may fail, slowing growth and increasing competitive vulnerability to full-suite providers.
- New products and market expansions may face acceptance, technical, and operational challenges; service disruptions could damage reputation, limit growth, and delay or prevent investment payback.
- Ongoing success depends on rapid innovation and effective enhancements across payments, point-of-sale, financial, and marketing services amid fast-evolving technologies (e-commerce, mobile, NFC/contactless, cryptocurrencies, tokenization).

It details exposure to chargebacks and refunds from payment card fraud and seller disputes, noting the EMV liability shift since October 2015, the fact that not all offered readers are EMV-compliant, the absence of seller reserves, and occasional decisions not to seek reimbursement—factors that could lead to losses, network fines, higher fees, or termination of card processing. Finally, it stresses the need to continually innovate amid rapid changes in e-commerce, mobile commerce, proximity payments (including NFC), cryptocurrencies, and tokenization; failure to deliver effective enhancements and features could materially and adversely affect the business.

title: Substantial and increasingly intense competition in our industry may harm our business.
heading: Substantial and increasingly intense competition in our industry may harm our business.
start_phrase: We compete in markets characterized by vigorous competition, changing technology, changing seller and buyer needs, evolving industry standards, and frequent introductions of new products and services.
summary:
- Risk of technological obsolescence: New services and technologies could surpass or impair current offerings; significant time and cost to integrate new tech with uncertain ROI and market acceptance.
- Innovation constraints: Development may be hindered by industry standards, payment network rules, laws and regulations, customer resistance to change, and third-party intellectual property.
- Dependence on third parties: Company relies on external providers—including competitors—for access to and development of key technologies; failure to anticipate or respond to industry shifts could harm the business.
- Interoperability and ongoing updates: Products must work across diverse systems, devices, and infrastructures; continuous modifications are required, and delays or failures could reduce demand and seller satisfaction.
- Intensifying competition: Market features aggressive rivals, frequent product introductions, and evolving buyer/seller needs; larger competitors with more resources and trusted brands, M&A activity, and new entrants increase pressure.
- Customer acquisition challenges: Some sellers have exclusive or near-exclusive relationships with competitors, making it difficult or costly to win their business.
- Pricing pressure and margin compression: Competitors may cross-subsidize to offer lower prices; growing sellers seek customized/favorable pricing and incentives, which can further reduce gross profit.
- Reliance on payment card networks and processors: Acceptance of cards depends on networks (Visa, Mastercard, American Express, Discover) and bank/acquiring processors; limited direct network access heightens exposure to their rules and practices; processor agreements are multi‑year with upcoming expirations, posing continuity and terms risks.

title: We are dependent on payment card networks and acquiring processors, and any changes to their rules or practices could harm our business.
heading: We are dependent on payment card networks and acquiring processors, and any changes to their rules or practices could harm our business.
start_phrase: Our business depends on our ability to accept credit and debit cards, and this ability is provided by the payment card networks, including Visa, MasterCard, American Express, and Discover.
summary:
- Rapid technological change risk: New services/technologies could surpass or obsolete current offerings; integrating new tech may be costly, time-consuming, and may not yield timely returns or market acceptance. Industry standards, payment network rules, laws/regulations, user resistance, and third-party IP can inhibit innovation.
- Need for constant product enhancement and compatibility: Ongoing modifications required to interoperate with diverse mobile, software, communications, and database systems; delays or failures in updates, or third-party infrastructure changes, could reduce demand and customer satisfaction.
- Reliance on third parties for technology: Dependence on partners—including competitors—for new technologies increases execution risk if market developments are misread.
- Intensifying competition and pricing pressure: Numerous incumbents and new entrants with greater resources can outspend, innovate faster, cross-subsidize to offer lower prices, and leverage exclusive merchant relationships and stronger brands. Growing share of large sellers may force deeper discounts/incentives, compressing gross profit.
- Dependence on payment card networks and acquiring processors: Vulnerable to processor performance, contract renewals, preferential treatment of competing services, and changing/strictly interpreted network rules. Noncompliance can lead to fines or loss of card acceptance. Increases in interchange/assessment or processor fees can erode margins or force pricing model changes. Obligations to manage/register high-risk merchants carry penalty and termination risks.
- Volatile, seasonal quarterly results: Unpredictable operating metrics influenced by customer growth/retention, system investments, legal outcomes, margin dynamics, product adoption, expense timing, fraud/risk losses, outages, regulatory shifts and enforcement, macro conditions, weather, and retail patterns—affecting stock price predictability.
- Talent risk: Business growth depends on attracting, motivating, and retaining key management and skilled employees.

Changes or adverse interpretations may require costly operational adjustments; noncompliance could lead to fines, loss of incentives, higher costs, or being barred from processing cards.
- Fee and pricing risk: The company pays interchange fees, network assessments, and processor fees that can increase due to network decisions or regulation. Because sellers are charged a flat rate, fee changes can compress margins, reduce pricing competitiveness, or force pricing model changes. Contract renewals with processors/networks may occur on unfavorable terms or not at all.
- High‑risk merchant oversight: Failure to detect or prevent prohibited or high‑risk seller activity can result in penalties from card networks. The company must block or register such sellers and increase monitoring; future penalties could become material or jeopardize card acceptance, requiring onboarding process changes.
- Volatile quarterly performance and seasonality: Operating results and metrics fluctuate significantly and unpredictably, influenced by customer acquisition/retention, infrastructure investments, legal outcomes, margin performance, product adoption, expense timing, fraud/risk losses, system outages, regulatory changes and enforcement, macro conditions, weather, and retail buying patterns. These swings can adversely affect business predictability and Class A common stock price.
- Talent dependency: The business relies on key management and skilled employees; difficulties in attracting, motivating, and retaining talent could impair the company’s ability to operate, innovate, and grow.

title: We depend on key management, as well as our experienced and capable employees, and any failure to attract, motivate, and retain our employees could harm our ability to maintain and grow our business.
heading: We depend on key management, as well as our experienced and capable employees, and any failure to attract, motivate, and retain our employees could harm our ability to maintain and grow our business.
start_phrase: Our future success is significantly dependent upon the continued service of our executives and other key employees.
summary:
- Dependence on payment card networks, banks, and acquiring processors, with risks from non-renewal, unfavorable terms, degraded service, or preferential treatment of competitors.
- Exposure to changing and discretionary payment network operating rules; non-compliance or adverse interpretations could lead to fines, higher costs, required operational changes, or loss of card acceptance.
- Financial impact from increases in interchange fees, assessments, and processor fees; flat-rate pricing model heightens margin and competitiveness risk if fees rise or agreements aren’t renewed on reasonable terms.
- Liability for monitoring and controlling “high-risk” or non-compliant sellers; potential penalties, registration and oversight burdens, and possible termination of card acceptance.
- Significant and unpredictable quarterly fluctuations and seasonality in operating results and metrics, affecting stock price volatility.
- Drivers of variability include customer acquisition/retention, infrastructure upgrades, legal outcomes, margins, new product adoption, growth-related expenses, fraud and risk losses, system outages, regulatory changes/enforcement, macroeconomic shifts, weather, and retail buying patterns.
- Reliance on key executives and employees; talent attraction and retention challenges, especially in the competitive San Francisco Bay Area; potential disruption from management changes and increased compensation needs.
- Specific key-person risk related to the CEO’s divided time due to concurrent leadership at another company.
- Need to enhance operational, financial, and internal control systems to manage growth; risks from failing to scale processes, systems, and culture efficiently; potential higher costs and slower product development as the company grows.
- Sensitivity to macroeconomic downturns, particularly affecting small-business sellers through reduced spending, higher failure rates, fewer processed payments, increased chargebacks, and adverse impacts on lending programs (e.g., Square Capital) and related receivables.

heading: If we do not continue to improve our operational, financial and other internal controls and systems to manage growth effectively, our business could be harmed.

title: A deterioration of general macroeconomic conditions could materially and adversely affect our business and financial results.
heading: A deterioration of general macroeconomic conditions could materially and adversely affect our business and financial results.
start_phrase: Our performance is subject to economic conditions and their impact on levels of spending by businesses and their customers.
summary:
- Dependence on key executives and employees; loss of management or other key personnel could disrupt operations and growth, with added recruiting and training costs. Jack Dorsey’s concurrent CEO role at Twitter may limit his focus on the company.
- Intense competition for talent, especially in the San Francisco Bay Area, requiring significant cash/equity to attract and retain staff; failure to hire and retain effectively could harm strategy execution and growth. Post-IPO equity liquidity may make retention harder.
- Need to improve and scale operational, financial, and internal controls and systems to manage growth; challenges include upgrading administrative infrastructure, installing better management information and control systems, and preserving core values and strategy.
- Risk that scaling efforts require substantial investment and may slow feature development versus smaller competitors; poor growth management could impair competitiveness and objectives.
- Exposure to macroeconomic downturns that disproportionately affect small-business sellers, reducing payment volumes, increasing transaction and advance losses, and potentially increasing chargebacks after seller closures.
- Potential slowdown in Square Capital growth and performance: fewer qualifying sellers, declining MCA receivables, and business loans repaid more slowly or not at all during downturns.
- Investment portfolio risks (U.S. government and corporate securities) including credit, liquidity, market, and interest rate risks; prolonged market declines or downgrades could trigger impairments and hurt financial results.
- Importance of maintaining and promoting the brand through effective, cost-efficient marketing; product or policy changes customers dislike, or ineffective campaigns, could harm the brand and results.
- Dependence on third-party advertising platforms (Google, Twitter, Facebook); changes in their operations, pricing, or terms could raise costs or reduce acquisition effectiveness.
- Vulnerability to negative or inaccurate media coverage and misinformation that can damage brand and adoption; legal limits may constrain responses during certain periods.
- Global expansion plans entail significant time and resources and carry risks: difficulty attracting enough sellers, misjudging competitive conditions, localization and translation costs, IP and data protection challenges, potential need to alter business practices, lack of local acceptance, and integration with local third-party providers.

title: If we are unable to maintain, promote, and grow our brand through effective marketing and communications strategies, our brand and business may be harmed.
heading: If we are unable to maintain, promote, and grow our brand through effective marketing and communications strategies, our brand and business may be harmed.

title: Expanding our business globally could subject us to new challenges and risks.
heading: Expanding our business globally could subject us to new challenges and risks.
start_phrase: We currently offer our services and products in multiple countries and plan to continue expanding our business further globally.
summary:
- Macroeconomic and market risks: Deteriorating global credit/equity markets and adverse interest rate, liquidity, and credit conditions could slow merchant sales, delay or prevent loan repayments, and reduce the value of the company’s investment portfolio, potentially requiring impairment charges and harming financial results.
- Brand and marketing dependence: Growth relies on maintaining and promoting the brand through effective, cost‑efficient marketing and reliable, innovative products. Unpopular product changes, ineffective campaigns, or high acquisition costs could damage the brand and results. Visibility and customer acquisition are also vulnerable to pricing and policy changes on third‑party advertising platforms (e.g., Google, Twitter, Facebook).
- Reputational exposure: Negative or misleading media coverage about products, practices, management, privacy/security, litigation, or customer actions can erode trust, with limited ability to respond publicly due to legal constraints.
- Global expansion challenges: International growth requires significant resources and faces risks including limited seller adoption, unforeseen competition, localization costs (language, customs), IP and data protection challenges, business model adjustments, dependence on local partners, entrenched competitors, staffing and cultural hurdles, self‑regulatory acceptance, complex and conflicting regulations (privacy/security, anti‑bribery), tariffs/sanctions, FX volatility, complex and changing tax regimes, and regional economic/political instability. These factors may impede successful expansion and overall growth.
- Reliance on third parties for critical payment services: Operations depend on card networks, acquiring processors, issuers, banking partners (including for lending and P2P services), and payment systems (e.g., ACH) for data transmission, chargebacks, refunds, and fund settlement. Concentration among a few acquirers and potential service failures, errors, unfavorable terms, or difficult transitions to new providers pose material risks.
- Technology and platform interoperability: Services and hardware must integrate with third‑party operating systems, mobile devices, and web browsers. Changes by OS/browser providers that degrade functionality, add requirements, or favor competitors, as well as policy or design changes by app marketplaces (Apple App Store, Google Play), can hinder access, downloads, and usage, materially affecting the business.

title: Many of our key components are procured from a single or limited number of suppliers. Thus, we are at risk of shortage, price increases, changes, delay, or discontinuation of key components, which could disrupt and materially and adversely affect our business.
heading: Many of our key components are procured from a single or limited number of suppliers. Thus, we are at risk of shortage, price increases, changes, delay, or discontinuation of key components, which could disrupt and materially and adversely affect our business.
start_phrase: Many of the key components used to manufacture our products, such as the custom parts of our magstripe reader, including its magnetic stripe-reading element, its plastic cover, and its application-specific integrated circuits, come from limited or single sources of supply, as do the plastic cover, connector, and security cage of our contactless and chip reader.
summary:
- Dependency on third-party mobile platforms: Apple, Google, and other app marketplace operators may release software updates that do not work effectively with the company’s products and services, potentially reducing demand and causing seller/customer dissatisfaction.
- Hardware interoperability risks: Changes in mobile device design (e.g., Apple’s removal of the audio jack on iPhone 7) can limit compatibility with the company’s hardware (like magstripe readers), necessitating adapters or hardware modifications that may be costly or resisted by merchants.
- Concentrated supply base: Many key components (e.g., magnetic stripe-reading elements, plastic covers, ASICs, connectors, security cages) are sourced from single or limited suppliers; some products are assembled by a single contract manufacturer using custom tools kept at their facilities.
- Contract and procurement limitations: Supplier and manufacturer agreements often auto-renew but can be non-renewed; there are limited firm commitments on component quantities and timelines, creating exposure to shortages and delays.
- Component availability risks: Off-the-shelf parts may be modified, discontinued, or become unavailable on reasonable terms; the company is still identifying alternative manufacturers for assembly and single-sourced components.
- Manufacturing disruption risks: Potential issues include equipment breakdowns, labor strikes or shortages, natural disasters, material shortages, and cost increases.
- Supply chain and logistics vulnerabilities: Port strikes or shutdowns, transit/storage loss or damage, intellectual property theft, and tampering can constrain product supply.
- Business impact: Interruptions, cost increases, or delays in components/manufacturing can impair timely product delivery, damage seller relationships, hinder new seller acquisition, and materially and adversely affect the business.

title: Our business could be harmed if we are unable to accurately forecast demand for our products and to adequately manage our product inventory.
heading: Our business could be harmed if we are unable to accurately forecast demand for our products and to adequately manage our product inventory.
start_phrase: We invest broadly in our business, and such investments are driven by our expectations of the future success of a product.
summary:
- Risks from inaccurate demand forecasting and inventory management: long lead times (e.g., Square Reader) require early supplier orders; underestimates cause product shortages that damage brand, seller relationships, and growth; overestimates create excess/obsolete inventory, write-downs, discounts, and gross profit pressure. Demand is influenced by competitor activity, market shifts, and economic conditions.
- Dependence on third-party suppliers and contract manufacturers—many overseas—limits control over production quality and timing; defects can trigger negative publicity, government investigations, litigation, recalls, and financial exposure, with no assurance of supplier reimbursement.
- Product and service reliability risks: software, hardware, and system errors (including from frequent updates and third-party integrations) can disrupt complex, high-volume payment processing, causing settlement delays, oversettlement, reporting errors, and lost fees, which have occurred previously.
- Cybersecurity threats: third-party breaches, cyber-attacks, and identity theft can enable unauthorized access to sensitive data, disrupt services, or degrade functionality; evolving attack techniques may evade detection and prevention, harming sellers, reputation, and creating significant liability.
- Hardware design/manufacturing issues can lead to consumer safety problems, recalls, redesigns, redistribution, and inventory shortages, along with regulatory inquiries and lawsuits.
- Operational resilience risks: system failures, service interruptions, delays, and catastrophic events affecting our or sellers’ service availability could harm our business and brand and result in substantial liability.

- Risks that products and services may not function as intended due to software, hardware, and systems errors, manufacturing defects, security breaches, or human error; limited control over overseas manufacturers can impact quality; frequent updates increase error risk; failures can disrupt payment processing (e.g., delayed settlements, oversettlement, reporting errors, fee collection issues), damage customer businesses, and lead to negative publicity, investigations, and litigation.

- Vulnerability to systems failures, service interruptions, delays, and catastrophic events that disrupt availability of company or seller products/services, harming the business and brand and potentially resulting in substantial liability.

title: Square Capital is subject to additional risks relating to the availability of capital, seller receivables payments, availability and structure of its bank partnership and general macroeconomic conditions.
heading: Square Capital is subject to additional risks relating to the availability of capital, seller receivables payments, availability and structure of its bank partnership and general macroeconomic conditions.
start_phrase: Square Capital, which includes our wholly owned subsidiary Square Capital, LLC, is subject to risks in addition to those described elsewhere in this Annual Report on Form 10-K.
summary: The excerpt outlines significant operational, financial, and regulatory risks. It emphasizes vulnerability to service interruptions from cyberattacks, human error, and natural disasters (notably in the seismically active San Francisco Bay Area), noting limited redundancy, potentially inadequate disaster recovery, insufficient insurance, and increasing regulatory scrutiny of business continuity that could divert resources. It warns that outages and performance degradation can lead to revenue loss, high remediation costs, reputational damage, customer attrition, and potential claims. It details specific risks to Square Capital, including reliance on third-party investors to purchase bank-originated loans, sensitivity to pricing and servicing fees, exposure to adverse macroeconomic conditions that can increase defaults and reduce seller eligibility, limited recourse on seller breaches, and dependence on a bank partner amid regulatory and litigation scrutiny of partnered lending; losing or changing that partnership could necessitate costly alternatives or a reversion to MCAs. The text also highlights plans to explore new credit models that may require additional licenses, partnerships, or capabilities, with the risk that evolving regulations could hinder growth. More broadly, the company is subject to extensive, changing domestic and international laws across consumer protection, privacy/data protection, fair lending, financial services, labor, and marketing, with potential for audits, investigations, fines, and burdensome compliance. It underscores growing obligations around collection, use, security, and transfer of personal data, the costs of compliance with privacy/security standards, and the business impact of any real or perceived noncompliance. Finally, it notes complex, evolving regulatory regimes governing payments and financial services, including banking, lending, deposit-taking, money transmission, foreign exchange, and payment services.

title: Our business is subject to extensive regulation and oversight in a variety of areas, all of which are subject to change and uncertain interpretation.
heading: Our business is subject to extensive regulation and oversight in a variety of areas, all of which are subject to change and uncertain interpretation.
start_phrase: We are subject to a wide variety of local, state, federal, and international laws, regulations, and industry standards in the United States and in other countries in which we operate.
summary:
- Highlights credit and fraud risks tied to Square Capital, including potential mispricing of loans and servicing exposures that could materially harm the business.
- Describes reliance on a Utah‑chartered, FDIC‑insured industrial bank to originate loans and notes growing regulatory and litigation scrutiny of bank–fintech partnered lending arrangements.
- Warns that loss or deterioration of the bank partnership, or inability to secure alternatives or licenses, could force a shift to other models (e.g., MCA), causing delays, costs, and adverse impacts.
- Notes plans to explore additional credit models and structures that may require new procedures, partnerships, licenses, or capabilities; failure to adapt or burdensome new rules could impede growth.
- Emphasizes extensive, evolving, and uncertain regulatory obligations across multiple jurisdictions, covering consumer protection, privacy, fair lending, financial services, labor/employment, trade, competition, data protection, and marketing, with risks of investigations, fines, injunctions, and costly compliance.
- Details increasing obligations around collection, use, retention, security, and transfer of personal data for employees, sellers, and customers, with divergent global standards that raise compliance complexity and costs.
- Acknowledges significant expenses for privacy/security compliance and the risk that real or perceived failures (including deviations from posted privacy policies) could reduce product usage and harm the business.
- Notes complex and evolving regulations and licensing for payments and financial services, including banking, lending, deposit‑taking, money transmission (domestic and cross‑border), foreign exchange, and payment services.

title: Our business is subject to complex and evolving regulations and oversight related to our provision of payments services and other financial services.
heading: Our business is subject to complex and evolving regulations and oversight related to our provision of payments services and other financial services.
start_phrase: The laws, rules, regulations, and licensing schemes that govern our business include or may in the future include those relating to banking, lending, deposit-taking, cross-border and domestic money transmission, foreign exchange, payments services
summary:
- Square Capital risks: exposure to borrower non-payment and fraud; underwriting and pricing errors; reliance on a Utah-chartered, FDIC-insured bank partner amid regulatory scrutiny of bank–fintech partnerships; potential disruption if the partner exits or terms change, possibly forcing a return to MCA or a new partnership; exploration of new credit models that may require additional licenses, partnerships, or capabilities; evolving regulations could constrain growth.

- Broad regulatory exposure: subject to extensive, changing, and variably interpreted local, state, federal, and international laws covering consumer protection, privacy/data protection, fair lending, financial services, labor and employment, immigration, import/export, product labeling, competition, and marketing/communications; noncompliance (actual or perceived) may trigger audits, investigations, fines, injunctions, and costly compliance burdens.

- Data privacy and security: obligations around collection, use, retention, security, and transfer of personal data for employees, sellers, and their customers; significant compliance costs; failure to meet posted policies or legal requirements could reduce product use and harm the business.

- Payments and financial services regulation: applicable regimes include banking, lending, deposit-taking, domestic/cross-border money transmission, foreign exchange, payment processing/settlement, consumer financial protection, anti–money laundering, escheatment, and PCI DSS; oversight by multiple U.S. regulators (e.g., Treasury, CFPB, FDIC, state/local agencies) and foreign regulators (e.g., METI in Japan, AUSTRAC in Australia); expansion increases regulatory obligations; transition from MCAs to bank-facilitated loans adds federal and state lending requirements; expanding Payroll implicates additional tax and employment rules.

- Compliance and enforcement risk: despite a growing compliance program, the company may face fines, penalties, lawsuits, asset forfeiture, enhanced licensing requirements, mandated business changes, reputational damage, customer loss, and legal liability; could be required to cease or modify operations in certain jurisdictions or obtain additional approvals.

- Money transmitter licensing: holds required licenses but faces obligations on safeguarding customer funds, reporting, bonding, and inspections; definitions and scope of money transmission can shift; prior fines highlight interpretive risk; future sanctions or licensing hurdles could force operational changes, exits from certain markets, or costly product modifications.

- Litigation exposure: ongoing and potential claims across IP, consumer protection, privacy, labor/employment (including class actions over Caviar courier classification and expense reimbursement), immigration, trade, labeling, competition, accessibility, securities, tax, marketing, and commercial disputes; growth and public company status increase frequency and stakes; legal frameworks are evolving and may not have anticipated the company’s business models, creating uncertainty.

title: We are subject to risks related to litigation, including intellectual property claims and regulatory disputes.
heading: We are subject to risks related to litigation, including intellectual property claims and regulatory disputes.
start_phrase: We may be, and have been, subject to claims, lawsuits (including class actions and individual lawsuits), government investigations, and other proceedings involving intellectual property, consumer protection, privacy, labor and employment, immigration, import and export practices, product labeling, competition, accessibility, securities, tax, marketing and communications practices, commercial disputes, and other matters.
summary:
- The company operates in a heavily regulated payments and financial services environment, including PCI DSS, anti-money laundering, escheatment, and consumer financial protection, overseen by multiple U.S. regulators (Treasury, CFPB, FDIC, state/local) and foreign regulators (e.g., Japan’s METI, Australia’s AUSTRAC), with regulatory exposure increasing as it expands internationally.
- Square Capital’s shift from merchant cash advances to bank-partnered loans adds federal and state lending requirements; expanding Square Payroll would trigger additional tax and regulatory obligations.
- Despite an expanding compliance program, the company faces risks of fines, penalties, enforcement actions, increased licensing demands, mandated business changes, reputational harm, customer loss, remediation costs, and legal liability from actual or perceived non-compliance.
- As a licensed money transmitter, the company is subject to fund investment restrictions, reporting, bonding, and inspections; regulatory interpretations of what constitutes money transmission can change, and past fines indicate ongoing risk of investigations, sanctions, required operational changes or exits in certain jurisdictions, and costly or unattainable licensing.
- Litigation and regulatory dispute risks span intellectual property, consumer protection, privacy, labor and employment (including Caviar courier contractor classification class actions), immigration, trade, labeling, competition, accessibility, securities, tax, marketing/communications, and commercial disputes; risks grow with scale and public-company status amid evolving, uncertain laws.
- Potential litigation outcomes include high costs, management distraction, injunctions halting operations, unfavorable settlements or judgments, compelled licensing on unfavorable terms, forced development of alternatives or discontinuation of technology/products, substantial payments, or operational cessation.
- Intellectual property is critical yet vulnerable: reliance on patents, trademarks, copyrights, trade secrets, and contracts may not prevent infringement, misappropriation, or invalidation; protection is costly and weaker in some foreign jurisdictions; as of December 31, 2016, the company held 229 issued patents and 588 applications, but IP may not confer durable competitive advantage, and impairment could materially harm the business.
- The company notes a risk that it may be unable to secure future financing on favorable terms, or at all, to meet capital needs.

It emphasizes reliance on trade secrets, trademarks, copyrights, patents, domain names, and contractual protections (confidentiality and invention assignments), while noting these measures can be expensive, difficult to enforce, and may be breached, challenged, narrowed, invalidated, or circumvented—resulting in unauthorized disclosure, loss of competitive advantage, or adverse ownership claims. The passage cites an IP portfolio as of December 31, 2016 (229 issued patents, 588 pending) but cautions that issuance and effectiveness aren’t assured, registration efforts may fail or be uneconomical, and foreign jurisdictions may afford weaker protection, hampering international expansion. It concludes that significant impairments or limits on asserting IP rights could materially harm the business and separately flags the risk of being unable to secure future financing on favorable terms, or at all.

- Dependence on IP protection: Success relies on trade secrets, trademarks, copyrights, patents, domain names, and contractual protections with employees and partners; these measures may be insufficient, breached, or challenged, narrowing, invalidating, or rendering IP unenforceable.
- Trade secret vulnerabilities: Reliance on confidentiality and invention assignment agreements may fail, allowing unauthorized disclosure or use by competitors and adverse ownership claims by individuals not under assignment agreements.
- Limitations and costs of global IP protection: Obtaining and enforcing IP rights is expensive and difficult, particularly abroad where protections may be weaker; defending IP internationally may require significant resources with no assurance of success.
- IP portfolio context: As of December 31, 2016, the company held numerous issued patents and pending applications, but there is no assurance applications will issue or that rights confer competitive advantages.

- Capital and financing risks: The company may need additional capital and may be unable to secure debt or equity on favorable terms or at all; existing and future credit facilities may impose restrictive covenants, with potential defaults accelerating repayment obligations.
- Dilution risk: Future equity or convertible issuances could dilute existing stockholders and introduce senior rights over current Class A common stock.

title: Any acquisitions, strategic investments, entries into new businesses, divestitures, and other transactions could fail to achieve strategic objectives, disrupt our ongoing operations, and harm our business.
heading: Any acquisitions, strategic investments, entries into new businesses, divestitures, and other transactions could fail to achieve strategic objectives, disrupt our ongoing operations, and harm our business.
start_phrase: In pursuing our business strategy, we routinely conduct discussions and evaluate opportunities for possible acquisitions, strategic investments, entries into new businesses, divestitures, and other transactions.
summary:
- Liquidity and financing: Historically funded via equity financings, bank credit facilities, and capital leases; only recently generating sufficient operating cash flow with no assurance of continuation. May need additional capital for opportunities, refinancing, surety bonds, acquisitions, or unforeseen events; may be unable to obtain debt or equity on favorable terms or at all.
- Debt covenants and default risk: Existing credit facility includes operating covenants (limits on indebtedness and liens, restrictions on inter-company transactions, caps on dividends and stock repurchases). Noncompliance—potentially due to factors beyond control—could trigger defaults and acceleration of debt.
- Dilution and capital structure: Future equity or convertible debt issuances could significantly dilute existing stockholders and may carry senior rights and preferences to Class A common stock. Inability to secure financing could constrain growth and responsiveness to business challenges.
- M&A and strategic transactions: Ongoing evaluation of acquisitions, investments, new business entries, divestitures. Limited acquisition experience; such transactions can divert management, incur costs, and face risks including: failure to advance strategy or deliver returns; integration challenges (technology, IT, accounting, culture, personnel); loss of key talent; inadequate compliance controls at targets and due diligence gaps; added legal/financial exposure; customer/partner retention issues; unknown liabilities (including litigation); regulatory constraints (e.g., competition laws); and potential dilution or added debt.
- Divestitures: Potential difficulties in executing timely, favorable sales; challenges separating businesses; possible revenue loss, margin pressure, delays in strategic goals, higher costs, relationship disruptions, and unforeseen obligations and liabilities.
- Accounting standards risk: Changes in U.S. GAAP or related interpretations by FASB, the SEC, or other bodies could materially affect reported financial results, including past transactions.
- Tax risks: Exposure to higher-than-expected tax liabilities across multiple jurisdictions; subject to audits and potential disagreements with tax authorities; changes in tax laws/rates could increase liabilities; complex, judgment-heavy global tax provisioning may lead to variances that materially affect results.
- Dual-class governance risk: Class B common stock carries 10 votes per share vs. one for Class A, concentrating voting control with pre-IPO holders (including executives, employees, directors). As of Dec 31, 2016, Class B holders had ~89.3% of voting power; executives/directors and affiliates held ~60.8%. Class B converts to Class A when aggregate Class B voting power falls below 5% and generally upon transfer (with limited exceptions), which over time can further concentrate relative voting power among long-term Class B holders.

- Exposure to higher-than-expected tax liabilities due to audits and disputes across U.S. and foreign jurisdictions, as well as adverse changes in tax laws, rates, or regulations; complexity and judgment in global tax provisioning may lead to differences between estimates and actual liabilities.
- Ownership and governance risks from a dual-class share structure concentrating voting power with pre-IPO holders (including executives, employees, directors, and affiliates), with Class B shares carrying ten votes per share versus one for Class A.
- As of December 31, 2016, holders of Class B stock controlled the vast majority of voting power, significantly limiting the ability of other stockholders to influence corporate matters.
- Mechanics of Class B conversion: automatic conversion to Class A when Class B falls below 5% of combined voting power; most transfers trigger conversion to Class A (with limited exceptions), increasing the long-term relative voting power of remaining Class B holders.

summary:
- Covers Item 3: Legal Proceedings and Item 4: Mine Safety Disclosures.
- States the company is currently involved in, and may in the future face, various litigation matters, including intellectual property disputes and government investigations.
- Details a class action related to the Caviar business alleging misclassification of couriers as independent contractors, leading to violations of California Labor and Business & Professions Codes (e.g., requiring couriers to bear business expenses).
- Procedural history: The court compelled arbitration of Jeffry Levin’s individual claims (Nov 16, 2015) and dismissed the lawsuit with prejudice (May 2, 2016). Levin appealed the arbitration order to the Ninth Circuit; briefing completed by Dec 21, 2016, and the parties await a hearing date.
- PAGA developments: Levin dropped his PAGA claim; new PAGA-only action filed by couriers Nadezhda Rosen and La’Dell Brewster in California state court on Nov 7, 2016, seeking statutory penalties for alleged misclassification. Caviar’s time to respond extended to Mar 17, 2017. A February 2017 mediation occurred without full agreement.
- Notes additional ordinary-course litigation matters where exposure cannot be reasonably estimated; the company does not currently expect a material adverse effect on overall financial condition or liquidity but cautions outcomes are uncertain and could be material to a particular period.
- Item 4: Mine Safety Disclosures—Not applicable.

heading: Item 6. Selected Financial Data
start_phrase: The following selected consolidated statement of operations data for the years ended December 31, 2016 , 2015 , and 2014 , and the consolidated balancesheet data as of December 31, 2016 , and 2015 , have been derived from our audited consolidated financial statements and should be read in conjunction with thesection titled “Management’s Discussion and Analysis of Financial Condition and Results of Operations” and our consolidated financial statements and relatednotes included elsewhere in this Annual Report on Form 10-K.
summary:
- Compares cumulative total return since 11/19/2015: Square, Inc. index rose from 100 to 104.28 by 12/31/2016 versus S&P 500 at 110.52 and S&P North American Technology at 111.15.
- Presents Item 6 Selected Financial Data (2012–2016), including:
  - Revenue breakdown: transaction-based, Starbucks transaction-based, subscription and services-based, and hardware.
  - Total net revenue grew to $1.71B in 2016 (from $1.27B in 2015 and $0.85B in 2014); subscription/services and hardware expanded rapidly from small bases.
  - Cost of revenue components (transaction-based, Starbucks, subscription/services, hardware, amortization of acquired technology) and resulting gross profit ($576.0M in 2016).
  - Operating expenses by function (product development, sales/marketing, G&A, transaction/loan/advance losses, amortization of acquired customer assets; 2013 impairment), yielding operating losses each year (2016: $(170.5)M).
  - Net losses each year; 2015 includes a deemed dividend on Series E preferred stock impacting net loss attributable to common stockholders.
  - Per-share basic/diluted net loss and growing weighted-average shares outstanding.
  - Share-based compensation by function, rising to $138.8M in 2016.
- Consolidated balance sheet data (2013–2016), highlighting:
  - Cash and equivalents of $452.0M (2016), growing total assets to $1.21B.
  - Working capital of $424.0M, settlements receivable of $321.1M, customers payable of $388.1M.
  - Stockholders’ equity increased to $576.2M in 2016.
- Key operating metrics and non-GAAP financial measures (excluding Starbucks impact):
  - Gross Payment Volume (GPV) rose to $49.7B in 2016 (from $35.6B in 2015).
  - Adjusted Revenue reached $686.6M in 2016.
  - Adjusted EBITDA turned positive at $44.9M in 2016 (negative in prior years).
  - Adjusted Net Income (Loss) per share improved to $0.04 (basic and diluted) in 2016.
  - Definitions provided for GPV and Adjusted Revenue; rationale for subtracting transaction-based costs and excluding Starbucks due to its transition to another provider.
  - Notes that most seller agreements are cancellable and generally not long-term.
- Non-GAAP methodology, rationale, and limitations:
  - Adjustments exclude Starbucks revenue/costs, non-cash items (amortization, share-based compensation), litigation settlement (Robert E. Morley; $48.0M in 2016), gains/losses on asset sales, and impairments.
  - Adjusted EBITDA also excludes depreciation, interest, other income/expense, and taxes.
  - Reconciliations provided from GAAP net loss to Adjusted EBITDA and to Adjusted Net Income (Loss), and per-share computations (basic/diluted; diluted equals basic when losses are anti-dilutive).
- Item 7 MD&A Overview of business and revenue recognition:
  - Describes Square’s commerce ecosystem: managed payments (swipe/dip/tap and online), analytics/reporting, next-day settlements, dispute management, PCI compliance; consumer product Square Cash.
  - Monetization via per-transaction fees recognized upon authorization, net of refunds.
  - Point-of-sale software/services for orders, inventory, locations, employees, payroll, customer engagement; monetized via transaction, subscription, or service fees.
  - Square Capital: facilitates seller loans; revenue recognized upon loan sale to investors or over time if held; servicing fees earned.
  - Caviar food ordering: revenue from restaurant fees, delivery and consumer service fees; recognized upon delivery, net of refunds.
  - Hardware (readers, Stand, peripherals): revenue recognized upon delivery, net of returns.
  - Serves millions of sellers across sizes and industries in the U.S., Canada, Japan, and Australia.

title: Management’s Discussion and Analysis of Financial Condition and Results of Operations
heading: Item 7. Management’s Discussion and Analysis of Financial Condition and Results of Operations
start_phrase: You should read the following discussion and analysis in conjunction with the information set forth under “Selected Financial Data” and our consolidatedfinancial statements and related notes included elsewhere in this Annual Report on Form 10-K.
summary:
- Scope and forward-looking statements: Management’s Discussion and Analysis (MD&A) outlining performance, liquidity, capital resources, risks, and uncertainties, to be read with the financial statements and Selected Financial Data.
- Business overview: Square’s commerce ecosystem combining managed payments, POS software, analytics, and hardware; ability to accept in-person (magstripe, EMV, NFC) and online payments; consumer offering via Square Cash. Monetization primarily through per-transaction fees, plus subscriptions and services.
- Ecosystem components and monetization:
  - Managed payments: reporting/analytics, next-day settlement, digital receipts, dispute/chargeback management, PCI compliance; revenue recognized net of refunds at authorization.
  - Software and services: Employee Management, Customer Engagement, Payroll, Appointments, Instant Deposit, Gift Cards, and Marketplace; monetized via subscription, service, or transaction fees.
  - Square Capital: transition in 2016 from merchant cash advances (MCAs) to bank-originated loans purchased by Square and largely sold to third-party investors; revenue from loan sale gains and ongoing servicing, plus recognition on retained loans held for sale; mitigates balance sheet risk.
  - Caviar: food ordering/delivery service; revenue from restaurant fees, delivery, and consumer service fees, recognized upon delivery net of refunds.
  - Hardware: contactless & chip readers, chip card readers, Square Stand, third-party peripherals; revenue recognized upon delivery; certain hardware (Stand; contactless & chip reader) priced below cost for strategic reasons.
- Geographic footprint: sellers across the U.S., Canada, Japan, and Australia; broad industry mix from small vendors to multi-location businesses.
- Key operating metrics and performance (2014–2016):
  - GPV grew from $23.8B (2014) to $35.6B (2015) to $49.7B (2016).
  - Total net revenue rose from $850.2M (2014) to $1.27B (2015) to $1.71B (2016).
  - Adjusted Revenue increased from $276.3M (2014) to $452.2M (2015) to $686.6M (2016).
  - Net loss attributable to common stockholders narrowed to $(171.6)M in 2016 from $(212.0)M in 2015; Adjusted EBITDA turned positive in 2016.
- Revenue and cost presentation updates: renaming of line items to transaction-based revenue/costs (including Starbucks), and subscription and services-based revenue/costs to better reflect monetization; underlying components unchanged.
- Detailed revenue drivers:
  - Transaction-based revenue up 39% in 2016 on 39% GPV growth; continued positive dollar-based retention and new seller additions.
  - Starbucks transaction-based revenue declined 45% in 2016 and ceased after Starbucks’ full transition to another processor by Q4 2016.
  - Subscription and services-based revenue up 123% in 2016 (to 8% of total), driven by Square Capital and Caviar, with contributions from newer services like Instant Deposit.
  - Hardware revenue up 171% in 2016, led by contactless & chip reader shipments post-2015 launch.
- Cost of revenue and margins:
  - Transaction-based costs tracked GPV growth; Starbucks costs fell faster than Starbucks revenue in 2016 due to higher processing rates paid by Starbucks from Oct 2015.
  - Subscription/services costs increased with Caviar scale and amortization of developed products.
  - Hardware costs up with volumes, but improved mix (contactless & chip reader versus Stand) benefited margins.
  - Amortization of acquired technology increased due to prior acquisitions.
- Operating expenses and notable items:
  - Product development is the largest expense; increased with engineering/product/design hiring and higher share-based compensation (SBC).
  - Sales and marketing rose with headcount, Square Cash P2P costs; paid marketing stable in 2016; expectation of S&M declining as a percentage of revenue long term.
  - General and administrative increased significantly in 2016 due to scaling support functions, first-year public company costs, higher third-party services, and a non-recurring $48M litigation settlement related to Robert E. Morley (Q1 2016).
  - Transaction, loan, and advance losses decreased in 2016 despite GPV growth due to improved risk operations and data science; historical transaction losses ~0.1% of GPV (2014–2016). No loss exposure on loans sold to third parties; retained loans at lower of cost or fair value with fair value exceeding cost; MCA receivables still carried with allowances.
  - Amortization of acquired customer assets declined in 2016 as certain assets reached end of life.
- Interest and taxes:
  - Net interest/other swung to slight net income in 2016 due to interest on marketable securities and FX fluctuations.
  - Provision for income taxes decreased in 2016; 2015 increase tied to reduced tax benefits from acquisitions.
  - 2015 included a $32.2M deemed dividend on Series E preferred stock (non-recurring).
- Quarterly results and trends:
  - Eight-quarter tables include revenue/costs, expenses, SBC by function, and non-GAAP metrics (Adjusted Revenue, Adjusted EBITDA, Adjusted Net Income (Loss)) with reconciliations.
  - Seasonality: strongest transaction-based revenue in Q4, weakest in Q1 (holiday-driven GPV); subscription/services and hardware show less seasonality, with hardware tied to product launches/promotions.
  - G&A includes $50M litigation expense in Q1 2016, later settled.
- Liquidity and capital resources:
  - Year-end 2016: $452.0M cash and cash equivalents; $87.3M marketable securities; restricted cash of $36.7M; total cash, equivalents, and investments of $539.3M.
  - Cash flows (2016): operating +$23.1M; investing $(122.7)M (marketable securities purchases, capex); financing +$90.7M (equity proceeds from option/warrant/ESPP exercises).
  - IPO in Nov 2015 provided $245.7M net proceeds; historical funding through preferred stock pre-IPO.
  - Undrawn $375.0M revolving secured credit facility maturing Nov 2020; variable interest terms; customary fees.
  - Transition from MCAs to bank-originated loans (purchased and largely sold to investors) completed in Q1 2016; small retained loan balances.
  - Management believes liquidity is sufficient for at least 12 months; may pursue additional financing as needed.
  - Restricted cash supports letters of credit for processing and lease collateral; working capital fluctuates daily with GPV and period-end timing.
- Contractual obligations and commitments:
  - Operating leases through 2025; capital leases; purchase commitments to hardware suppliers; schedule of payments presented.
  - No off-balance sheet arrangements.
- Critical accounting policies and estimates: revenue recognition; accrued transaction losses; valuation of loans held for sale; business combinations; goodwill and intangible assets; income taxes; share-based compensation. Emphasis on estimates and judgment under GAAP.
- Market risk disclosures (Item 7A):
  - Interest rate sensitivity: limited impact due to short-duration investments; ability to hold to maturity; potential floating-rate exposure if drawing on credit facility.
  - Foreign currency risk: most revenue in USD; operating exposure in JPY, CAD, AUD; FX fluctuations can affect results.

Trends
Transaction-based
 revenue is highly correlated with the level of GPV generated by sellers using our managed payments services. Historically ourtransaction-based
 revenue has been strongest in our fourth quarter and weakest in our first quarter, as our sellers typically generate additional GPV during theholiday
 season. We believe that this seasonality has affected and will continue to affect our quarterly results; however, to date its effect has been masked by ourrapid
 growth. Starbucks transaction-based revenue continued to decline throughout 2016, and, during the fourth quarter of 2016, Starbucks completed itspreviously announced transit
ion to another payments solution provider and accordingly we do not expect revenue from Starbucks to recur in the future.Subscription
 and services-based revenue generally demonstrates less seasonality than transaction-based revenue. The sequential increase is primarilydriven by continued growth and expansion o
f Square Capital and Caviar.58
Hardware revenue generally demonstrates less seasonality than transaction-based revenue, with most fluctuations tied to periodic product launches,promotions, or other arrang
ements with our retail partners.Changes in
 product development expenses primarily reflect the timing of additions of engineering, product, and design personnel. To a lesser extent, theyalso
 reflect the timing of fees and supply costs related to maintenance and capacity expansion at third-party data center facilities, development and tooling costsrelated
 to the design, testing, and shipping of our hardware products, and fees for software licenses, consulting, legal, and other services that are directly related togrowing and maintaining our produc
ts and services.Changes
 in sales and marketing expenses reflect the variable nature of the timing and magnitude of paid marketing and customer acquisition initiativesacross
 our advertising channels. Changes in sales and marketing expenses are also affected by the timing of additions of direct sales, account management, local,product
 and paid marketing, retail and ecommerce, partnerships, and communications personnel. Additionally, sales and marketing expenses are affected by thetiming
 and magnitude of costs related to our Square Cash peer-to-peer service and the total shipments of our magstripe readers in a given period, as they includethe cost of manufactur
ing and distributing those readers.Changes
 in general and administrative expenses primarily reflect the timing of additions of finance, legal, risk operations, human resources, andadministrative

here is no minimum time frame during which the cash must remain restricted.Long-term restricted cash of 
$14.6 million  as of  December 31, 2016 reflects cash deposited into money market  accounts that is used as collateral pursuantto

ets as the terms extend beyond one year.We
 experience significant day-to-day fluctuations in our cash and cash equivalents, settlements receivable, and customers payable, and hence workingcapital. These fluctuations
 are primarily due to:•
Timing of period end.  For  periods that end on a weekend or a bank holiday, our cash and cash equivalents, settlements receivable, and customers payableamounts typically will be 
more than for periods ending on a weekday, as we settle to our sellers for payment processing activity on business days; and•
Fluctuations in daily GPV.  When  daily GPV increases, our cash and cash equivalents, settlements receivable, and customers payable amounts increase.Typically
 our cash, cash equivalents, settlements receivable, and customers payable balances at period end represent one to four days of receivables anddisbursements to be made in 
the subsequent period. Customers payable and settlements receivable balances typically move in tandem, as pay-out and pay-in largely occur on
 the same business day. However, customers payable balances will be greater in amount than settlements receivable balances due to thefact
 that a subset of funds are held due to unlinked bank accounts, risk holds, and chargebacks. Holidays and day-of-week may also cause significantvolatility in daily GPV amounts.

 of interest rate changes and foreign currency fluctuations.

- Market risk (Item 7A):

- Independent auditor’s report: KPMG LLP audited Square, Inc.’s internal control over financial reporting (ICFR) as of December 31, 2016.
- Framework and standards: Evaluation based on COSO’s Internal Control – Integrated Framework (2013) and conducted under PCAOB (U.S.) standards.

- Definition and limitations: Describes what ICFR encompasses and notes inherent limitations and that effectiveness may change over time.
- Opinion: Square, Inc. maintained effective ICFR, in all material respects, as of December 31, 2016, per COSO 2013.
- Related financial statement audit: KPMG also audited the consolidated financial statements for the three years ended December 31, 2016, and issued an unqualified opinion dated February 24, 2017.
- Auditor details: KPMG LLP, San Francisco, California; report dated February 24, 2017.

start_phrase:
Square,

summary:

- Business description: Square provides an integrated commerce ecosystem including managed payments, POS, hardware, software, loans, payroll, the Square Cash app for peer-to-peer transfers, and the Caviar food-ordering service. Founded in 2009, headquartered in San Francisco with offices in the U.S., Canada, Japan, and Australia.
- Out-of-period adjustment to transaction loss reserves: In Q2 2016, Square recorded a $6.0 million adjustment to correct prior understatement of the reserve for transaction losses ($0.5M related to Q1 2016, $2.6M to 2015, $1.6M to 2014, $1.3M to earlier periods). At December 31, 2015, cash and cash equivalents decreased by $9.5M with an equal increase to customer funds; no change to current assets, total assets, or net loss. The 2015 cash flow statement was revised to reduce cash from operations and change in cash and cash equivalents by $6.5M. Determined immaterial under SAB 99.
