title: Subscription and services-based revenue
heading: 7.1.8.2 Subscription and services-based revenue
start_phrase: Subscription and services-based revenue primarily consists of revenue related to services provided through software offerings or deriving from the use ofunderlying data.
summary:
- Overview of revenue streams and related cost recognition for subscription and services, hardware, and transaction-based activities.
- Subscription and services-based revenue:
  - Generated primarily from Square Capital, Caviar, and software-as-a-service (SaaS)/data offerings.
  - Square Capital:
    - Transitioned from merchant cash advances to bank-originated loans in Q1 2016.
    - Loans are originated by a Utah-chartered, FDIC-insured industrial bank; the company purchases the loans, acquiring all rights.
    - Sellers are charged a one-time origination fee by the bank based on risk (derived mainly from processing activity); loans have no stated coupon.
    - The company intends to sell certain loans to third-party investors for an upfront fee; it records the purchase cost of loans and recognizes gain on sale upon transfer of title.
    - The company services the sold loans and earns servicing fees, recognizing servicing revenue as services are performed.
    - For loans not sold, revenue is recognized as a portion of expected seller repayments over the loan cost, in proportion to principal reductions.
  - Caviar:
    - Facilitates restaurant food delivery via a courier order management app.
    - Revenue from restaurant (seller) fees, delivery fees, and consumer service fees; recognized upon delivery, net of refunds.
  - SaaS:
    - Fees for stand-alone software usage recognized ratably over the service period.
- Hardware revenue:
  - From sales of contactless and chip readers, chip card readers, Square Stand, and third-party peripherals.
  - Recognized upon delivery to end customer when title and risk of loss transfer; recorded net of returns.
  - Deferred revenue recorded for advance payments prior to delivery.
- Cost of revenue:
  - Transaction-based and Starbucks transaction-based costs:
    - Include interchange to issuing banks, network assessment fees, third-party processor fees, and bank settlement fees.
    - Processor contracts typically have 2–4 year terms.
  - Subscription and services-based costs:
    - Primarily Caviar-related payments to third-party couriers and seller-facing equipment.
    - Also include amortization of developed subscription/services products.
  - Hardware costs:
    - Product costs for readers, Square Stand, and peripherals, including manufacturing overhead and personnel, royalties, packaging, and fulfillment.

 receivable represents amounts due from third-party payment processors for customer transactions.

Additions recorded in transaction and advance losses; charge-offs reduce the allowance. No loss exposure on MCAs sold to third-party investors under existing arrangements.

Liability accreted and asset depreciated. As of Dec 31, 2016: ARO liability $3.2m (gross of accretion); associated asset $2.6m (net of depreciation).
- Business combinations: Purchase price allocated to identifiable assets and liabilities at fair value; excess is goodwill. Adjustments during the measurement period (up to one year) offset goodwill; afterward, adjustments flow through the income statement.
- Long-lived assets and finite-lived intangibles: Tested for recoverability when indicators arise using undiscounted cash flows; impairments measured to fair value (DCF, market data, third-party appraisals). No impairment charges recorded for the periods presented.
- Goodwill: Tested annually on December 31 and more frequently if needed; impairment recognized if carrying amount exceeds reporting unit fair value. Option to perform a qualitative assessment to determine if a quantitative test is necessary.

title: Long-Lived Assets, including Goodwill and Acquired Intangibles
heading: 7.1.26 Long-Lived Assets, including Goodwill and Acquired Intangibles
start_phrase: The Company evaluates the recoverability of property and equipment and finite lived intangible assets for impairment whenever events or circumstances indicate that the carrying amounts of such assets may not be recoverable.
summary:
- Asset disposals: When assets are retired or disposed, their cost and accumulated depreciation are removed from the accounts, and any gain or loss is recorded in operating expenses.
- Capitalized internal-use software: Costs are capitalized once criteria are met; prior costs are expensed. Capitalized amounts are recorded in property and equipment and amortized straight-line over the software’s useful life, recognized in product development or allocated to subscription/service costs. Disclosures include amounts capitalized and amortized for 2014–2016.
- Leases: The company has non-cancellable capital and operating leases; rent is recognized on a straight-line basis. Leasehold improvements are capitalized and depreciated over the lesser of lease term or asset life; landlord allowances reduce rent expense straight-line. Cash payments for improvements are investing cash flows; landlord reimbursements are operating cash flows.
- Asset retirement obligations (AROs): The company records ARO liabilities at estimated fair value with an offsetting asset, using assumptions about legal obligations, timing, amounts, discount, and inflation rates; liabilities are accreted and assets depreciated. ARO balances at December 31, 2016 are disclosed.
- Business combinations: Purchase price is allocated to identifiable assets and liabilities at fair value; excess is goodwill. Adjustments within the measurement period (up to one year) adjust goodwill; afterward, changes flow through the income statement.
- Long-lived assets impairment: Property, equipment, and finite-lived intangibles are tested for recoverability upon indicators of impairment using undiscounted cash flows; impairments reflect excess of carrying value over fair value determined via valuation techniques. No impairments recorded in the periods presented.
- Goodwill impairment: Tested annually (December 31) or upon triggering events, with an optional qualitative assessment to determine if a quantitative test is needed. No goodwill impairments recorded in the periods presented.
- Acquired intangibles: Include acquired technology and customer relationships. Technology is amortized in cost of revenue; customer relationships are amortized in operating expenses. Useful lives are reassessed periodically.
- Customers payable: Liability for amounts owed to sellers net of the company’s earned revenue, including timing differences (typically settled within one business day), risk management holds, and amounts for customers without linked bank accounts.
- Accrued transaction losses: Reserve for expected chargebacks and fraud, estimated using current data, expected future chargebacks, and historical loss trends. Additions impact current operations; realized losses are charged against the reserve and presented within transaction and advance losses.
- Recent accounting pronouncements:
  - ASC 606 Revenue: Effective for fiscal years beginning after Dec 15, 2017; the company will adopt using the modified retrospective approach, not early adopting, and is assessing financial statement and systems impacts.
  - ASU 2015-11 Inventory: Measures inventory at lower of cost and net realizable value, effective for fiscal years beginning after Dec 15, 2016; impact under evaluation.
  - ASU 2015-17 Deferred taxes: Requires classification of all deferred tax assets and liabilities as noncurrent, effective for fiscal years beginning after Dec 15, 2016.

title: Customers Payable
heading: 7.1.27 Customers Payable
start_phrase: Customers payable represents the transaction amounts, less revenue earned by the Company, owed to sellers.

title: Accrued Transaction Losses
heading: 7.1.28 Accrued Transaction Losses
start_phrase: The Company establishes a reserve for estimated transaction losses due to chargebacks, which represent a potential loss due to disputes between a seller and their customer or due to a fraudulent transaction.
summary:
- Goodwill: Company performs a qualitative impairment assessment to determine if the two-step test is needed; concluded it was not necessary and recorded no impairment charges for the periods presented.
- Intangible assets: Acquired intangibles include technology and customer relationships from acquisitions. Acquired technology is amortized straight-line within cost of revenue; customer relationships are amortized straight-line within operating expenses. The Company reassesses useful lives regularly for potential revisions.
- Customers payable: Liability for amounts owed to sellers net of revenue earned, including timing differences due to next-day settlement, funds held per risk management policies, and amounts held for customers without linked bank accounts.
- Accrued transaction losses: Reserve for chargebacks and fraudulent transactions based on available data, expected future chargebacks, and historical loss rates. Additions recorded in current operations; charges made when losses are recognized. Classified within transaction and advance losses on the income statement.
- Recent accounting pronouncements:
  - ASU 2014-09 (Revenue from Contracts with Customers) and related updates: Core principle of recognizing revenue upon transfer of goods/services for expected consideration. Effective for fiscal years after Dec 15, 2017. Company will not early adopt, plans modified retrospective adoption, and is assessing financial statement impact and system changes.
  - ASU 2015-11 (Simplifying the Measurement of Inventory): Measure inventory at lower of cost and net realizable value. Effective for fiscal years after Dec 15, 2016; Company evaluating impact.
  - ASU 2015-17 (Balance Sheet Classification of Deferred Taxes): Classify all deferred tax assets and liabilities as noncurrent. Effective for fiscal years after Dec 15, 2016.

rent disclosures.In

title: Deemed Dividend on Series E Preferred Stock
heading: 7.14.3 Deemed Dividend on Series E Preferred Stock
start_phrase: On November 24, 2015, upon the closing of the IPO, certain holders of Series E preferred stock were issued an incremental 10,299,696 shares of Class B common stock pursuant to the Company's Restated Certificate of Incorporation dated as of September 8, 2014, as amended (the 2014 Certificate).
summary:
- Deemed dividend from Series E preferred stock: Upon the November 24, 2015 IPO, an adjustment under the 2014 Restated Certificate triggered issuance of 10,299,696 additional Class B shares to certain Series E holders. The IPO-related adjustment created a beneficial conversion feature (treated as a deemed dividend), measured as the difference between the commitment-date fair value of the common stock issued and the original proceeds from Series E. The company recorded a one-time $32.2 million deemed stock dividend, increasing net loss to arrive at net loss attributable to common stockholders.
- Common stock structure and rights: The company has Class A and Class B common stock; both classes are entitled to dividends when declared, but none were declared as of December 31, 2016. Voting rights are one vote per Class A share and ten votes per Class B share. Class B is generally convertible into Class A upon transfer. There are no preemptive, subscription, redemption, or sinking fund rights. Authorized shares as of December 31, 2016: 1,000,000,000 Class A and 500,000,000 Class B, each with a $0.0000001 par value. Outstanding shares as of December 31, 2016: 198,746,620 Class A and 165,800,756 Class B.
- Warrants: Under an August 7, 2012 processing agreement with Starbucks (amended through 2015), the company issued warrants for up to 15,761,575 shares subject to performance conditions; 6,304,620 were canceled in 2015. As of December 31, 2016, outstanding warrants covered 9,456,955 shares at a weighted-average exercise price of approximately $11.01 per share.
- Stock compensation plans: The 2015 Equity Incentive Plan (effective November 17, 2015) succeeded the 2009 Stock Option Plan; existing 2009 awards remain under their original terms. The 2015 Plan authorizes ISOs, NSOs, restricted stock, RSUs, performance shares, and stock bonuses at no less than fair market value on grant date. Initially 30,000,000 shares were reserved, with recycling of shares from the 2009 Plan upon expiration/forfeiture/repurchase. An annual “evergreen” increases the reserve by the least of 40,000,000 shares, 5% of outstanding shares as of the prior fiscal year-end, or a smaller amount set by the board. As of December 31, 2016, 19,295,512 options and RSUs were outstanding under the 2015 Plan, and 36,282,753 shares were available for future issuance.

title: Restricted Stock Activity
heading: 7.14.8 Restricted Stock Activity
start_phrase: The Company issues restricted stock units (RSUs) under the 2015 Plan, which typically vest over a term of four years.
summary:
- Describes the Company’s equity compensation programs, including the 2009 Stock Plan (ISOs/NSOs), the 2015 Plan for RSUs, and the 2015 Employee Stock Purchase Plan (ESPP).
- 2009 Plan: options must be granted at or above fair market value; standard vesting of 25% after one year then monthly over four years; 10-year contractual term; early exercise permitted with Company repurchase rights on unvested shares. Approximately 69.4 million options and RSUs were outstanding under the 2009 Plan as of December 31, 2016. The plan was closed to new issuances effective November 17, 2015.
- CEO share contribution: in January 2015, the CEO returned about 5.07 million common shares to the Company for retirement to mitigate dilution from future equity issuances.
- Stock option activity for 2016: starting balance 107.5 million; 1.8 million granted (weighted average exercise price $13.49); 24.3 million exercised ($3.39); 11.7 million forfeited/canceled ($10.98); ending balance 73.3 million at a $7.70 weighted average exercise price, 7.28-year weighted average remaining term, and $443.7 million aggregate intrinsic value. Options vested/expected to vest were 69.5 million; exercisable options were 69.9 million. Aggregate intrinsic value realized on exercises was $202.6 million (2016), $49.8 million (2015), and $47.8 million (2014). Weighted average grant-date fair value of options granted: $5.80 (2016), $5.87 (2015), $3.84 (2014).
- RSUs under the 2015 Plan typically vest over four years; a special grant of about 1.85 million RSUs on December 18, 2015 vested within one year. 2016 RSU activity: 3.63 million unvested at 12/31/2015; 17.06 million granted; 3.39 million vested; 1.86 million forfeited; 15.44 million unvested at 12/31/2016 (weighted average grant-date fair value $12.09).
- ESPP effective November 17, 2015: employees may contribute up to 15% of eligible compensation to purchase shares at 85% of the lower of the price at the start of the offering or at purchase. Twelve-month offering periods with two purchase periods; annual share pool increase equals the least of 8.4 million shares, 1% of outstanding shares, or an amount set by the administrator. As of December 31, 2016, 1,852,900 shares purchased and 5,696,594 shares available; ESPP-related share-based compensation expense was $5.1 million (2016) and $0.7 million (2015).
- Share-based compensation measurement: RSUs valued at market price on grant; options and ESPP valued using Black-Scholes-Merton with assumptions for expected term (simplified method), peer-based volatility, U.S. Treasury risk-free rate, expected dividends, and estimated forfeitures; expense recognized on a straight-line basis net of estimated forfeitures. Non-employee awards are initially measured at grant and remeasured over vesting; expense has been immaterial.
- Plan modification effective August 31, 2015: extended post-termination exercise term for NSOs for employees with at least two years of service; related incremental expense included $2.6 million (2016) and $3.3 million (2015).

heading: 7.14.9 Employee Stock Purchase Plan
start_phrase: On November 17, 2015 , the Company’s 2015 Employee Stock Purchase Plan (ESPP) became effective.
summary:
- RSU activity for the year ended December 31, 2016:

  - Granted: 17,060,055 RSUs ($12.08)

- Employee Stock Purchase Plan (ESPP):
  - Effective November 17, 2015; 12-month offering periods with two purchase periods per offering
  - Eligible employees can contribute up to 15% of eligible compensation
  - Purchase price is 85% of the lower of the stock price at the start of the offering or end of the purchase period
  - First offering ran from November 19, 2015 to November 15, 2016

Employee
Stock
Purchase
Plan
On  
November 17, 2015 , the Company’s 2015 Employee Stock Purchase Pl an (ESPP) became effective. The ESPP allows eligible employees to purchaseshares
 of the Company’s common stock at a discount through payroll deductions of up to 15%  of their eligible compensation, subject to any plan limitations. TheESPP
 provides for 12  -month offering periods. The offering periods are scheduled to start on the first trading day on or after May 15 and November 15 of eachyear,
 except for the first offering period, which commenced on November 19, 2015 and ended on November 15, 2016. Each offering period includes two  purchaseperiods,
 which begin on the first trading day on or after November 15 and May 15, and ending on the last trading day on or before May 15 and November 15,respectively.
  Employees are able to purchase shares at 85%  of the lower of the fair market value of the Company’s common stock on the first trading day of theoffering period
 or the last trading day of the purchase period. The number of shares available for sale under the ESPP will be increased annually on the first day ofeach
 fiscal year, equal to the least of (i) 8,400,000  million  shares, (ii) 1%  of the outstanding shares of the Company’s common stock as of the last day of theimmediately preceding fiscal year,
 or (iii) such other amount as determined by the administrator.As of 
December 31, 2016 ,  1,852,900 shares had been purchased under  the ESPP and 5,696,594  shares were available  for future issuance under the ESPP.The
 Company recorded $5.1  million and  $0.7 million of  share-based compensation expense related to the ESPP during the year ended December  31, 2016 and 2015 
, respectively.

Share-Based
Compensation
The
 fair value of RSUs is based on the market value of the Company's common stock on grant date. The fair value of stock options and employee stockpurchase
 plan  shares  granted  to  employees  is  estimated  on  the  date  of  grant  using  the  Black-Scholes-Merton  option  valuation  model.  This  share-basedcompensation
 expense valuation model requires the Company to make assumptions and judgments regarding the variables used in the calculation. These variablesinclude
 the expected term (weighted average period of time that the options granted are expected to be outstanding), the expected volatility of the Company’sstock, expected risk-free
 interest rate, expected dividends, and the estimated forfeitures of unvested stock options. To the extent actual forfeiture results differ fromthe
 estimates, the difference will be recorded as a cumulative adjustment in the period estimates are revised. The Company uses the simplified calculation ofexpected
 term, as the Company does not have sufficient historical data to use any other method to estimate expected term. Expected volatility is based on anaverage
 of the historical volatilities of the common stock of several entities with characteristics similar to those of the Company. The expected risk-free rate isbased
 on the U.S. Treasury yield curve in effect at the time of grant for periods corresponding with the expected life of the option. Expected forfeitures are basedon
 the Company’s historical experience. Share-based compensation expense is recorded net of estimated forfeitures on a straight-line basis over the requisiteservice period.
The
 fair value of stock options granted to non-employees, including consultants, is initially measured upon the date of grant and remeasured over thevesting

 the contractual term and share-based compensation expense is recognized on a straight-line basis over this term. Share-based compensation expense related tonon-employees has not been ma

heading: 7.16.2 Litigation
start_phrase: The Company is currently a party to, and may in the future be involved in, various litigation matters (including intellectual property litigation), legal claims, and government investigations.
summary:
- Commitments and contingencies – leases:
  - Non-cancelable operating leases for office space expire between 2017 and 2025. Rental expense was $11.3 million (2016), $12.8 million (2015), and $11.4 million (2014).
  - Future minimum payments as of December 31, 2016 (in thousands): Operating leases total $116,703 (2017: $16,639; 2018: $16,519; 2019: $15,673; 2020: $15,757; 2021: $16,172; thereafter: $35,943). Capital leases total $1,882; less interest $4; present value $1,878; current portion $691; non-current portion $1,187.
  - Sublease income was $3.1 million (2016) and $0.6 million (2015) from non-cancelable subleases expiring in 2018.

- Litigation:
  - Caviar courier misclassification: A class action filed March 19, 2015 (Levin v. Caviar, Inc.) alleged misclassification and related California Labor Code/Business & Professions Code violations. The court compelled arbitration of individual claims (Nov 16, 2015) and dismissed the lawsuit with prejudice (May 2, 2016). Plaintiff appealed the arbitration order to the Ninth Circuit; briefing completed in December 2016; hearing date pending.
  - PAGA claims: Following stipulation, new PAGA-only action filed by Rosen and Brewster on Nov 7, 2016 in California state court, alleging courier misclassification and seeking statutory penalties; Caviar’s response deadline extended to March 17, 2017. Mediation occurred in February 2017; no final agreement on all material terms.
  - Other matters: The company is involved in additional routine litigation and disputes; cannot reasonably estimate exposure. Believes ultimate liabilities are not expected to be materially adverse overall, but outcomes could be material to results in a particular period.

- Segment and geographical information:
  - The company operates as a single operating and reportable segment; the CODM reviews consolidated financial information.
  - Revenue by geography (based on merchant billing address; in thousands):
    - United States: $1,643,852 (2016), $1,224,566 (2015), $825,578 (2014)
    - International: $64,869 (2016), $42,552 (2015), $24,614 (2014)
    - Total net revenue: $1,708,721 (2016), $1,267,118 (2015), $850,192 (2014)
    - No single international country contributed more than 10% of total revenue in 2014–2016.
  - Long-lived assets by geography (in thousands) at December 31:
    - United States: $162,118 (2016), $168,583 (2015)
    - International: $2,675 (2016), $2,114 (2015)
    - Total: $164,793 (2016), $170,697 (2015)

Litigation
The
 Company is currently a party to, and may in the future be involved in, various litigation matters (including intellectual property litigation), legalclaims, and government inv
estigations.The
 Company is involved in a class action lawsuit concerning independent contractors in connection with the Company’s Caviar business. On March 19,2015,
 Jeffry Levin, on behalf of a putative nationwide class, filed a lawsuit in the United States District Court for the Northern District of California against theCompany’s
 wholly owned subsidiary, Caviar, Inc., which, as amended, alleges that Caviar misclassified Mr. Levin and other similarly situated couriers asindependent contractors 
and, in doing so, violated various provisions of the California Labor Code and California Business and Professions Code by requiring themto
 pay various business expenses that should have been borne by Caviar. The Court compelled arbitration of Mr. Levin’s individual claims on November 16, 2015and
 dismissed the lawsuit in its entirety with prejudice on May 2, 2016. On June 1, 2016, Mr. Levin filed a Notice of Appeal of the Court’s order compellingarbitration
 with the United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit. Mr. Levin filed his opening appellate brief regarding the order compelling arbitration ofhis
 individual claims on October 7, 2016. The Company filed its answering brief on December 7, 2016, and Mr. Levin filed his reply on December 21, 2016. Theparties
 now await notice of a hearing date from the Ninth Circuit. Mr. Levin also sought an award of penalties pursuant to the Labor Code Private AttorneysGeneral
 Act of 2004 (PAGA). The parties stipulated that Mr. Levin would no longer pursue this PAGA claim but that it may instead be pursued by a differentcourier. 
Subsequently, couriers Nadezhda Rosen and La’Dell Brewster filed a new PAGA-only claim in California state court on November 7, 2016. Plaintiffsclaim
 that Caviar misclassified its couriers as independent contractors resulting in numerous violations of the California Labor Code, pursuant to which plaintiffsseek statutory penalties for those violations. The parties ha
ve stipulated to extend the time for Caviar to respond to the complaint until March 17, 2017. In February 2017,
 the Company participated in a mediation with the parties in these Caviar misclassification suits to explore resolution of the matters at hand; however, anagreement on all the material terms 
has not been reached.101
In addition, from time to time, the Company is involved in various other litigation matters and disputes arising in the ordinary course of business. TheCompany 
cannot at this time  fairly estimate a reasonable range of exposure, if any, of the potential liability with respect to these other matters. While the Companydoes
 not believe, at this time, that any ultimate liability resulting from any of these other matters will have a material adverse effect on the Company's results ofoperations,
 financial position, or liquidity, the Company cannot give any assurance regarding the ultimate outcome of these other matters, and their resolutioncould be material to 
the Company's operating results for any particular period, depending on the level of income for the period.

summary:
- Execution and signatures: Annual Report on Form 10-K for Square, Inc. signed February 24, 2017 by Jack Dorsey (President, CEO, Chairman). Power of Attorney authorizes Jack Dorsey, Sarah Friar, and Hillary Smith to sign amendments.  
- Signatories: CEO Jack Dorsey; CFO Sarah Friar; Chief Accounting Officer Ajmere Dale; Directors Roelof Botha, Paul Deighton, Jim McKelvey, Mary Meeker, Ruth Simmons, Lawrence Summers, and David Viniar (all dated February 24, 2017).  
- Exhibit Index: Lists charter documents (Amended and Restated Certificate of Incorporation and Bylaws), stock certificate form, Investors’ Rights Agreement, Starbucks warrant, multiple management and compensatory plans (2015 Equity Incentive Plan and ESPP, 2009 Stock Plan, Executive Incentive Compensation Plan, Outside Director Compensation Policy, Change of Control and Severance Agreements), executive offer letters (Jack Dorsey, Sarah Friar, Dana Wagner, Françoise Brougher, Alyssa Henry, Hillary Smith), key commercial agreements (office lease, revolving credit agreement, commitment letter, development/manufacturing/supply agreements with TDK, Cheng Uei, and ON Semiconductor), subsidiaries list, auditor consent, SOX 302/906 certifications, and XBRL exhibits. Notes indicate exhibits that are management/compensatory (+), confidential treatment requests (#), and that Exhibit 32.1 certifications are furnished, not filed.  
- Outside Director Compensation Policy (Exhibit 10.6, effective October 26, 2016):  
  - Cash retainers: $40,000 annual; additional retainers for committee roles—Audit & Risk chair $20,000; Compensation chair $15,000; Nominating & Corporate Governance chair $10,000; Audit member $10,000; Compensation member $5,000; Nominating & Corporate Governance member $2,500. Paid quarterly in arrears; no per-meeting fees.  
  - Equity: Directors may receive non-ISO awards under the 2015 Equity Incentive Plan. Option to elect fully vested RSUs in lieu of cash retainers, with specified election/revocation timing and blackout restrictions.  
  - Automatic nondiscretionary RSU grants: Initial Award pro-rated to $250,000 based on time since last annual meeting; Annual Award of $250,000 at each annual meeting; additional $70,000 RSU for Lead Independent Director. Vesting on the earlier of one year from grant or next annual meeting; full vesting upon Change in Control. Board may revise/suspend the policy.  
- Offer letter to Hillary Smith (Exhibit 10.13, dated 10/27/2016):  
  - Position: General Counsel reporting to Jack Dorsey; at-will employment.  
  - Compensation: $350,000 annual salary; $100,000 sign-on bonus at first paycheck and an additional $100,000 at one-year anniversary if still employed; potential repayment if voluntary termination within 12 months.  
  - Equity: Recommended grant of 600,000 RSUs under the 2015 Plan; 25% vests at one year from vesting commencement, then 1/16 quarterly, subject to approval.  
  - Conditions/terms: Confidential Information and Invention Assignment Agreement; restrictions on outside activities; tax withholding; proof of work authorization; background check; eligibility for Change of Control and Severance Agreement; mandatory binding arbitration in San Francisco with class/representative action waiver. Accepted by Hillary Smith; signed by Jacqueline D. Reses; anticipated start date 12/5/2016.  
- Subsidiaries (Exhibit 21.1): Square Capital, LLC (Delaware) and Caviar, Inc. (Delaware); additional subsidiaries omitted as not significant per Reg S-K.  
- Auditor consent (Exhibit 23.1): KPMG LLP consents to incorporation by reference into Form S-8 filings; references audit of 2016/2015 financials and internal control over financial reporting; dated February 24, 2017.  
- CEO/CFO certifications:  
  - SOX 302 (Exhibits 31.1 and 31.2): Jack Dorsey and Sarah Friar certify review of the 10-K, fair presentation, and effectiveness of disclosure controls and internal control over financial reporting, and disclose any changes, deficiencies, or fraud.  
  - SOX 906 (Exhibit 32.1): Jack Dorsey and Sarah Friar certify compliance with Exchange Act requirements and fair presentation of financial condition/results.  
- XBRL exhibits: Instance, schema, calculation, definition, labels, and presentation linkbases included.
